name: generative-recommenders-hr10
review_status: pending — priors.json and surface.json need a human read before this pack is trusted (README.md has the checklists)

guardrail.rule: hr@10 up by more than 0.005 while ndcg@10 is down by more than 0.004 is a re-ranking, not a better model: one or two newly hit targets pushed other hits down the list. Record it as a regression on position and do not spend the next round extrapolating from it.

role.hr@10: primary — the number the gate compares against the frozen baseline, the axis the ranking's `best` is chosen on, and the first column of the README's published tables
role.ndcg@10: guardrail — ranked on the frontier and read as a constraint: position-sensitive credit for the same hit, so it fails when a change reorders without improving
role.hr@50: diagnostic — recorded so an analysis can say whether a miss was near (11–50) or far; never ranked, because at 50 almost every method is above 0.5 and the metric stops discriminating
role.ndcg@50: diagnostic — same reason, and the pair (hr@50 − hr@10) is the useful derived view: whether the gain came from depth of the list or from the head
role.mrr: diagnostic — the README and train.py log it; it is NDCG@10 with a different weighting and adds no independent axis
role.train_seconds: cost — written by the metric reader; recorded, never optimised
role.gpu_hours: cost — charged by the ledger, never an objective: the loop's budget gate reads it

window.why: train.py evaluates every epoch but truncates an epoch's eval to `partial_eval_num_iters` batches unless `epoch % full_eval_every_n == 0`, and logs 'Truncating epoch N eval to M iters to save cost..' when it does. A truncated number is measured on a different, shuffled subset of the eval loader — incomparable between candidates and incomparable to the README's rows, which are full evals. The ML-1M configs leave `full_eval_every_n` at its default of 1, so every epoch is full there; the Amazon config sets 5, so four of five are not.
window.read_from: the stdout line `rank 0: eval @ epoch N in T s: NDCG@10 ..., NDCG@50 ..., HR@10 ..., HR@50 ..., MRR ...` (train.py, 'eval per epoch'); never the `batch-stat (eval)` lines (one training batch, not the eval set) and never a tensorboard average over epochs
window.value_epoch: the last epoch that was not truncated
window.note: The window is part of the contract, not a reader detail: a candidate compared on a truncated epoch and a baseline measured on a full one produce a difference that belongs to the loader, and nothing downstream can tell that from a structural gain.

notes: **Why hr@10 is primary and ndcg@10 is the guardrail.** HR@10 answers one question — did the held-out target appear in the top ten — and nothing else, which makes it the cheapest metric to attribute to a structural change. NDCG@10 is that same event weighted by rank, so it can only move when HR@10 moves or when the ordering of hits changes; making it the constraint keeps a re-ranking from being read as a win. Both are 'up'; there is no metric in this contract that is better when lower.

**Where 0.005 and 0.004 come from.** They are one quarter of the smallest published structural gap on this pack's dataset, rounded to the 1e-3 grid. README 'ML-1M' table: HSTU 0.3097/0.1720 → HSTU-large 0.3294/0.1893, i.e. +0.0197 HR@10 and +0.0173 NDCG@10 for the one structural change the repository publishes end to end (2→8 blocks, 1→2 heads, dqk/dv 50→25 at item_embedding_dim 50). A quarter of the smaller of those, 0.004325, is 0.004; a quarter of the HR@10 gap, 0.004925, is 0.005. Below that, a difference is not worth a GPU hour; at or above it, the change is at least a fifth of the largest lever anyone has published for this repository.

**The tolerance is calibrated for ml-1m only.** Amazon Books runs an order of magnitude lower (HSTU HR@10 0.0416 in the README), so an absolute 0.005 there would be a 12% relative jump. A run pointed at another dataset must re-derive the floor from that dataset's published gap before the comparison means anything — `minimum_effective_delta` is a field of this pack's contract, not a constant of the loop.

**The kernel reads the tolerance now, and only the contract sets it.** `judge.compareMetric` takes the minimum effective delta of the metric it is comparing — 0 when a contract states none, which is a strict comparison — so a 0.003 move against this pack's 0.005 floor is `inconclusive` rather than an improvement, and a round that moves inside the floor does not reset the no-improvement streak. The number is this pack's; the loop carries no threshold of its own. (The loader still refuses a malformed one: a zero, or a metric the objectives do not rank.)

**Both published tables agree with the direction.** Every metric in README's ML-1M/ML-20M/Amazon tables is higher-better; nothing in this repository reports an error metric as a headline. A domain that did would need another analysis — a correction that lowers a loss is 'down', and that is a second `direction` the kernel refuses to guess.

**What the kernel reads, and what it does not.** `primary`, `direction`, `objectives`, `guardrail`, `minimum_effective_delta` and `window_mode` are resolved by `packages/core/lib/metric-contract.js`, once, for the ranking, the stop rules and the gate. `window_mode: "last"` is what that resolver uses to collapse a windowed series to one number per metric — the last full eval is the row the published tables report. `role` and `window` stay prose: `role` is handed to the prompts and the dashboard, and `window` describes which epochs the reader `run-metrics.py` accepts. Neither is parsed into a decision.
